questions.question: A text claiming to be your bank asks you to reply with a code you just received. You should…
options: Never share it: the code is only for you
questions.explanation: One-time codes are for you only.

questions.question: A stranger offers you £200 to let money pass through your bank account. This is…
questions.explanation: Money mules can be prosecuted and lose their bank accounts.

questions.question: Where can you forward a scam text for free in the UK?
questions.explanation: 7726 spells SPAM on a keypad.

questions.question: A Marketplace seller insists on a bank transfer and refuses PayPal Goods & Services. The main risk?
questions.explanation: Protected payment methods let you get money back if the item never arrives.

questions.question: Authorised Push Payment (APP) fraud is when…
options: You're tricked into sending the money yourself
A bank charges you by mistake
questions.explanation: You make the payment, tricked by someone posing as your bank, a seller or a friend.

questions.question: Which web address is most likely fake?
questions.explanation: Real UK government sites end in .gov.uk.

questions.question: After losing money to a scam, someone offers to recover it for an upfront fee. This is…
questions.explanation: Recovery scams target people who've already been scammed.

questions.question: A caller says they're from your bank and you're unsure. Safest move?
options: Call back the number they gave you
Hang up and call 159 or the number on your card
Ask them to read out your balance
questions.explanation: Scammers can fake caller ID.

questions.question: A website shows a padlock next to its address. That means…
options: Only that the connection is encrypted
questions.explanation: Scam sites can have padlocks too.

questions.question: Your bank will never ask you to…
questions.explanation: “Safe account” requests are always scams.

questions.question: Since October 2024, mandatory reimbursement for APP fraud victims covers most cases up to…
questions.explanation: Banks must reimburse most APP fraud victims up to £85,000, with some exceptions.

questions.question: A “Hi Mum” scam message usually…
options: Comes from a new number asking for urgent money
questions.explanation: Call the real person on their old number first.

questions.question: A text says your parcel has a £1.45 fee to pay via a link. Best move?
options: Treat it as a likely scam and check via the courier's official site
questions.explanation: Small fees are the hook to steal card details.

questions.question: Which is the strongest password habit?
options: Unique passwords or passphrases, a password manager and 2FA
questions.explanation: Reused passwords let one breach unlock everything.

questions.question: Two-factor authentication (2FA) means…
options: A second check, like a code or app approval, on top of your password
questions.explanation: Even if a password leaks, 2FA blocks most break-ins.

questions.question: A QR code sticker on a parking meter could be…
options: A “quishing” scam leading to a fake payment page
questions.explanation: Use the official app or the meter itself where possible.

questions.question: What can happen to someone caught acting as a money mule?
options: Prosecution, bank account closure and years of trouble getting credit
questions.explanation: Consequences can last for years.

questions.question: A ticket seller on social media only accepts bank transfer. Safer option?
options: Use official resale sites, or pay by credit card or PayPal Goods & Services
questions.explanation: Ticket scams thrive on unprotected payments.

questions.question: In the UK, you can report a suspicious email by forwarding it to…
questions.explanation: The National Cyber Security Centre runs this reporting service.

questions.question: Which is a classic romance-scam warning sign?
options: They're happy to video call early on
They never meet in person, have repeated emergencies and ask for money
They introduce you to their friends
questions.explanation: Never send money to someone you've only met online.

questions.question: An investment app shows big gains, but you must pay a “tax” or “fee” before you can withdraw. This is…
questions.explanation: Fake platforms invent fees to squeeze out more money.
